why: knowledge.py's load-bearing job is a rights/attestation gate (CLAUDE.md: commercial books stay metadata-only unless the user explicitly attests private-use rights) plus hash-checked revoke -- no RAG framework (llama-index/langchain/haystack) or generic caching pattern ships that. Its retrieval engine is already sqlite FTS5, the lean stdlib option listed as an 'alternative,' not a reinvention needing replacement. Swapping to a framework would rebuild the governance logic on top of it while adding heavy, embedding-oriented dependency trees a one-maintainer, offline-CI repo doesn't need.

alternatives.name: llama-index
alternatives.covers: Document loaders (PDF/EPUB/DOCX/more), chunking strategies, embeddings-based vector retrieval and query engines.
alternatives.gap: No rights-mode/attestation/consent gate, no source-hash revoke workflow; defaults toward embedding/API-based retrieval, not pure offline lexical search.
alternatives.cost: Free/open-source (MIT), heavy transitive deps, frequent breaking changes per 2026 comparisons.
alternatives.maturity: Actively developed, large user base, version churn (~0.12.x per late-2025/2026 sources).

alternatives.name: langchain retrievers
alternatives.covers: Document loaders + retriever abstractions (BM25Retriever, vectorstore retrievers) usable for keyword or embedding search.
alternatives.gap: Same governance gap: no rights/attestation logic, no revoke-by-hash; 2026 comparisons describe a 'complexity tax for simple RAG pipelines.'
alternatives.cost: Free/open-source (MIT); 350+ integrations is unneeded weight for a 32-source catalog.
alternatives.maturity: Most widely adopted (92k GitHub stars per search), actively maintained, heavier than needed here.

alternatives.name: haystack
alternatives.covers: Pipeline-based retrieval components (can wire BM25-style retrieval), pipelines serializable to YAML.
alternatives.gap: Same governance gap as above; aimed at production RAG services, not a single-user CLI knowledge catalog.
alternatives.cost: Free/open-source (Apache 2.0); still a full framework, more install weight than stdlib sqlite3.

alternatives.name: sqlite FTS5 + ripgrep
alternatives.covers: FTS5 IS the search engine knowledge.py already uses (confirmed working here); ripgrep gives instant unindexed text search with zero build step.
alternatives.gap: Nothing, for the search mechanism itself -- already adopted. Bare ripgrep alone has no rights schema, attestation/revoke, bm25 ranking, or domain/availability filtering.
alternatives.cost: Free; ripgrep is one static Windows binary; FTS5 ships inside stdlib sqlite3 (confirmed, sqlite 3.45.1).
alternatives.maturity: Both extremely mature and stable; effectively finished tools.

alternatives.name: Directory-caching of fetched pages
alternatives.covers: Persists previously fetched URLs/pages as local files, avoiding repeat network fetches.
alternatives.gap: No rights_mode/licensing metadata, no ranked/filterable search, no chunking, no attestation/consent/revoke -- solves a narrower problem.
alternatives.cost: Free, trivial to write; doesn't answer 'what am I legally allowed to keep and how do I search it.'
alternatives.maturity: n/a -- a pattern, not a specific maintained tool.

migration_loc: If swapped to llama-index/langchain: ~598 lines removed, ~120-200 new glue lines, plus ~150 lines of rights/revoke logic rebuilt (no framework has it) -- roughly break-even. Keep-ours: 0 changed.
what_ours_does: knowledge.py (598 lines): CLI (validate/attest/build/query/revoke) around catalog.json (32 sources) enforcing a rights schema (rights_mode, canonical_url, verified_at). build loads metadata into sqlite FTS5 always; private text (txt/md/html/epub/docx/pdf, chunked) only after a hash-checked attestation. query runs FTS5+bm25 search, rebuilds on hash change; revoke deletes a source's private chunks.
strongest_counterargument: The ~160-line hand-rolled extract_html/epub/docx/chunks block duplicates, less robustly, what llama-index/langchain document loaders already provide (better malformed-file handling, more formats, smarter chunk boundaries); wrapping ebooklib/python-docx there would cut real lines without touching the rights/attestation logic that is this file's actual reason to exist.
